strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 15 models, 3 datasets, 92 questions, and multiple elicitation methods with strong reproducibility documentation and promised open-source release
Important problem framing that shifts from single responses to distribution modeling, appropriately acknowledging intra-group disagreement and demographic diversity
Practical contribution showing simple supervised calibration improves alignment by 16.3% on average with convergence at just 5 labeled examples, enabling easy adoption

Methodologically sound with appropriate use of Wasserstein distance for ordinal data, proper train/dev/test splits, and thorough variance analysis showing calibration reduces standard deviation 1.62× on average

Thorough supporting analyses including out-of-domain generalization (Section 6.3), post-training effects (Section 7), demographic-specific alignment variations (Section 5), and minimal supervision requirements
Nuanced discussion acknowledging risks of essentializing demographics, biases in LLMs, and potential misuse with appropriate ethics statement
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core contribution is straightforward regression-based calibration, a well-established technique lacking innovation for top-tier venue; work reads as empirical benchmark rather than methodological advance

Insufficient analysis of critical finding that SD prompting fails to consistently improve alignment (67% of settings); lacks investigation into why certain prompts fail and what factors determine success, despite being RQ1

Key methodological choices lack justification: (1) per-answer-choice regression optimization unexplained with no ablation provided; (2) optimizing MSE instead of the Wasserstein distance evaluation metric never justified; (3) small sample sizes (4-6 examples per demographic) raise statistical power concerns and undermine demographic-level conclusions

Statistical power limitations acknowledged but not resolved: few significant differences at individual demographic level (Section 5.1); Table 3 demographic degradations marked as 'not statistically significant'; undermines confidence in RQ3 findings

Incomplete comparison with prior work: limited engagement with why results differ from Beck et al. (2024) and Hu & Collier (2024); no comparison with alternative calibration methods (temperature scaling, Platt scaling, etc.); log probability results only tested on 4 Llama models and relegated to appendix

Generalization concerns: out-of-domain calibration (Table 9) shows substantial performance degradation on unseen datasets; raises questions about real-world applicability when populations/surveys are new; unclear how to handle truly unseen demographic groups at test time

Essentializing demographics concern acknowledged but not resolved: distributional framing helps vs. single-response but doesn't address fundamental issue that demographics aren't deterministic of opinion; paper essentially treats demographics as primary factor despite acknowledging they're 'not at all the only factor'

Limited scope: only 92 questions (subsampled for cost), exclusively ordinal/Likert questions, no multiple-choice or open-ended questions; post-training analysis only examines OLMo family; no intersectional demographic analysis despite mentioning it as future work

Incomplete practical guidance: unclear how to select demographic groups to calibrate given budget constraints, when to use group-specific vs. aggregate calibration, what happens with new demographic groups, or how to handle continuous demographics

Analysis gaps: only 5.2% of settings where calibration decreases performance but minimal characterization of these failure cases; no ablation studies on normalization approach, linear vs. random forest tradeoffs, or train/dev/test split sensitivity

strengths: Addresses important practical problem of using LLMs for opinion surveys with comprehensive evaluation across 15 models and 3 datasets
Advances beyond prior work by evaluating full response distributions rather than single majority responses
Practical finding that 5 supervised examples suffice for calibration
Extensive demographic-level analysis and thorough reproducibility support (detailed prompts, appendices, code release)
Honest treatment of limitations and caveats in practitioner guidance
weaknesses: Core method (regression-based calibration) is standard ML with no novel contribution; simply applies existing calibration techniques to a new domain
Central finding that sociodemographic prompting fails contradicts motivation but receives only superficial analysis; no investigation into why SD prompting doesn't work or how to improve it

Miscalibration of LLM outputs is unsurprising; the 16.3% improvement mainly comes from scaling, not deep insight. Missing analysis of what types of miscalibration exist or why LLMs exaggerate demographic differences
Weak statistical analysis at demographic level with very small samples (4-6 per demographic) and few significant differences after Bonferroni correction, undermining differential effects claims
No comparison to simpler calibration baselines (temperature scaling, Platt scaling, isotonic regression); design choices (per-choice regression, MSE vs. alignment metric) lack justification
Practical applicability unclear: requiring 5+ supervised examples reduces LLM advantage; missing cost-benefit analysis of when collecting human supervision vs. more human data is preferable
Out-of-domain generalization limited (Table 9 shows significant performance drops); in-domain evaluation overstates effectiveness
Interesting findings (model-demographic interactions, post-training effects) lack investigation and explanation; RQ5 analysis superficial (one model family only)
Evaluation scope constrained by cost (only 92 questions, 2 per OQA/WVS category); ethical concerns about stereotype perpetuation receive only cursory treatment

strengths: Comprehensive and rigorous empirical evaluation across 15 models, 3 datasets, and 92 questions with clear practical value for opinion prediction and survey research
Important methodological advancement: evaluates LLM distributions rather than single responses, properly accounting for intra-group disagreement and supporting pluralistic alignment goals
Practical findings with high deployability: minimal supervision (5 examples) achieves near-optimal calibration, with 3-5x variance reduction across settings, making model selection less critical
Strong reproducibility practices including detailed prompts in appendices, promised open-source release, and comprehensive results enabling full replication

Rigorous experimental methodology with proper statistical testing (paired t-tests with Bonferroni correction), multiple seeds for low-data regimes, and appropriate metrics (Wasserstein distance) for ordinal responses
Honest and reflexive presentation with transparent ethics statement addressing stereotyping risks and clear limitations documentation including small per-demographic sample sizes
Extensive analysis across multiple dimensions: three elicitation methods, out-of-domain generalization, post-training effects, and granular per-demographic results (Section 5)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: calibration approach uses straightforward supervised regression (linear/random forest) to transform distributions per answer choice—methodologically incremental rather than innovative

Key negative finding insufficiently explained: sociodemographic prompting doesn't consistently improve alignment (only 67% of settings pre-calibration), contradicting intuition and prior work, with minimal investigation of causes or solutions

Insufficient mechanistic understanding of why calibration works: paper demonstrates effectiveness but provides limited insight into sources of LLM miscalibration (overconfidence? mode-seeking?), relying on inference rather than direct analysis

Fairness concerns inadequately addressed: while noting calibration helps some demographics more than others (Table 3), limited investigation of whether aggregate calibration harms under-represented groups with small samples—critical given demographic modeling risks

Per-demographic analysis undermined by acknowledged small sample sizes (4-6 examples per group): group-level claims lack direct statistical testing despite low power, particularly problematic for fairness conclusions

Inelegant regression design: per-answer-choice regression with post-hoc normalization is unprincipled; constrained joint optimization for proper distributions attempted but dismissed without investigation into why probabilistic constraints degraded performance

Essentializing sociodemographics concern addressed superficially: while ethics statement acknowledges the fundamental issue, the paper doesn't deeply engage with the problem that demographics alone don't determine opinions or its perpetuation through modeling choices
Log probability results showing comparable performance (87.6% vs 86.2% verbalized) relegated to appendix without explanation for preferring verbalized despite greater theoretical grounding
Post-training effects (RQ5) remain inconclusive with dataset-dependent patterns that lack interpretation, limiting practical guidance for practitioners
All datasets English-language with Western/US bias, somewhat overstating generality claims; dataset-specific effects not deeply analyzed

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 15 models, 3 datasets, and multiple elicitation methods with proper statistical testing, providing a valuable benchmark for the community
Important negative result: demonstrates that sociodemographic prompting alone does not consistently improve distributional alignment, contradicting implicit assumptions in prior work

Practical method with strong empirical results: supervised calibration improves alignment by 16.3% on average and works with minimal supervision (1-10 examples), with excellent reproducibility and promised open-sourcing
Insightful analysis showing calibration reduces variance 3-5x across settings (Figure 2), suggesting LLMs systematically exaggerate demographic group differences
Addresses the ecological fallacy by focusing on distributional alignment and intra-group disagreement rather than majority voting, well-motivated by pluralistic alignment goals
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core contribution is standard supervised regression, which is not a novel algorithmic advance. The paper is primarily an empirical benchmark study rather than a methods paper

Demographic-level results inadequately addressed: calibration improves some groups but degrades others (Table 5); single regression model creates unavoidable trade-offs. Per-group calibration mentioned only as future work despite being a natural extension

Generalization concerns limit practical applicability: out-of-domain results (Tables 11-12) show non-trivial drops (85.5% vs 87.6% in-domain); unclear whether practitioners need to recalibrate for new questions, requiring per-question labeled data collection

Limited mechanistic insight: lacks analysis of what transformations the regression learns or whether LLMs systematically over/under-estimate specific response options. Understanding of why SD prompting fails remains superficial

Weak demographic-level evaluation: Section 5.1 acknowledges 'few significant differences' at individual demographic level with only 4-6 examples per group, yet these fairness concerns receive only cursory discussion in main text

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 15 models, 3 datasets, and multiple elicitation methods
Demonstrates practical efficiency of calibration with minimal supervision (1-10 examples)
Careful statistical testing with appropriate corrections and multiple runs
Thorough analysis of effects on individual demographic groups
Strong commitment to reproducibility with detailed appendices and promised code release
Well-motivated problem formulation around distributional rather than majority alignment
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: applies standard regression-based calibration from existing literature without innovation
Unclear practical motivation: does not explain why use LLMs+calibration instead of survey data directly
Shallow mechanistic insights: documents that calibration works without explaining why or when
Methodological concern: splitting distributions into independent training pairs inflates dataset size and violates regression assumptions; not adequately justified
Critical unexplored trade-off: calibration improves some demographic groups while degrading others (Table 5), but this is not analyzed or explained
Loss-metric mismatch: trains on MSE but evaluates on Wasserstein distance alignment; unclear if optimization aligns with evaluation
Conflates SD prompting evaluation with calibration: RQ1 shows SD prompting is variable, but this is addressed by calibration without resolving underlying SD prompting concerns
Out-of-domain generalization degrades substantially, limiting practical applicability
Shallow analysis of key findings: Section 4.3 (CoT) based on 2 models and qualitative inspection; RQ3 per-group analysis uses only 4-6 examples per demographic
Missing critical baselines: no comparison to alternative calibration methods, fine-tuning LLMs directly, or simpler scaling approaches

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 15 models, 3 datasets, 92 questions, multiple elicitation methods with rigorous statistical testing and appropriate corrections
Addresses important problem of distributional alignment with demographic groups, moving beyond majority-vote responses to capture intra-group disagreement and reduce stereotyping
Practical supervised calibration approach shows consistent ~16.3% average improvement across diverse settings and remarkably works with only 1-10 examples (strong data efficiency)
Systematic investigation of five well-defined research questions with nuanced findings (e.g., SD prompting inconsistent, calibration reduces 3-5x variance across settings)
Reproducibility focus: detailed prompts, demographics, hyperparameters in appendices; promised open-source benchmark; clear methodology enabling community replication
Honest discussion of limitations including demographic essentialism risks, potential for misuse, and recognition that demographics don't fully determine opinions
Novel out-of-domain generalization analysis showing calibration trained on 2 datasets generalizes to held-out dataset (85-93% of settings improved)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Supervised calibration via regression is straightforward; contributions primarily empirical rather than methodological. Splitting distributions by answer choice and renormalizing is ad-hoc.
Insufficient mechanistic understanding of why calibration works: hypothesis about LLMs 'exaggerating differences' is intuitive but never rigorously tested; no analysis of learned transformations

Inadequate individual demographic analysis (RQ3): only 3 of many demographics examined with acknowledged low sample sizes (4-6 examples); aggregate regression doesn't optimize for individual groups; unclear when/why some degrade

Insufficient engagement with ethical implications: demographic essentialism risks mentioned briefly but not deeply explored; unclear if aggregate calibration reinforces stereotypes; mitigation beyond 'apply with care' lacking

Limited investigation of why SD prompting fails (RQ1): unclear if prompts are poorly designed or task is fundamentally flawed; 'overthinking' effect mentioned but not systematically studied across models
Evaluation metric not validated: Wasserstein distance justified for ordinal data but no comparison with alternative divergence measures; unclear if conclusions robust to metric choice
Post-training analysis (RQ5) limited to single model family (OLMo-2-7B) with incomplete understanding: why post-training improves alignment on WVS but hurts on WGM/OQA insufficiently investigated
Missing methodological comparisons: only compared with few-shot prompting; no comparison to other calibration approaches (temperature scaling, Platt scaling) or simple baselines (min-max scaling)
Reproducibility barriers: large number of API calls creates expense; computational costs not discussed; distributions extracted at 0% for some model-setting combinations (Table 17)
Scope limitations: primarily English, Western-centric datasets; only 15 models (rapid development may quickly date results); limited theoretical grounding connecting to calibration theory
